newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico ruling party faces tough fight in key state.
newsitem.headline: Mexico ruling party faces tough fight in key state.

text.p: President Ernesto Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) faces a tough three- way fight against two strong opposition parties in elections on Sunday in a key state surrounding Mexico City.

Voters in the State of Mexico, the ancient heartland of the Aztec empire, will choose 122 new mayors and 75 state deputies in the election, widely seen as a dry run for the first-ever election of a mayor for Mexico City next year. The capital has been governed until now by presidential nominees.

Mexico state is the most populous state in the country with 11.7 million residents and a large concentration of industry. Several of its biggest municipalities are part of the greater Mexico City urban sprawl.

Running on the slogan "We Are Change," the conservative National Action Party (PAN) was the most optimistic. It claimed that after Sunday's vote it would govern at least 36 municipalities that grouped half the state's population.
The left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) predicted winning 31 towns.

Zedillo's PRI has the most to lose -- a fact reflected in its defensive campaign slogans, "Change Can Also Be A Setback" and "With You We Can Improve." It currently runs 108 of the 119 existing municipalities, with the PAN holding six and the PRD five. Three municipalities are being contested for the first time.

Polls have put the three main parties all fairly close to each other in the state's five biggest municipalities -- the jewels of the contest, which concentrate between them more than 40 percent of the population.

But the PAN claims it has the best chance in the northwestern middle-class area of Naucalpan. The PRD has set its sights on the polluted working-class suburbs of Nezahualcoyotl and Ecatepec to the east while the PRI expects to hold the state capital Toluca and the industrial zone of Tlalnepantla.

Historian and political scientist Lorenzo Meyer predicted on Monday that division of the anti-government vote would probably allow the PRI to keep a majority of the town halls, even though it might fail to win 50 percent of the vote.
